content: Cyclamate is an artificial sweetener that was discovered in 1937 at the University of Illinois by a graduate student named Michael Sveda. Its sweetness was identified accidentally when Sveda, working on the synthesis of an anti-fever medication, placed his cigarette on the lab bench. Upon returning the cigarette to his mouth, he noticed the sweet taste of cyclamate. The patent for cyclamate was initially purchased by DuPont but was later sold to Abbott Laboratories. Abbott conducted the necessary studies and submitted a New Drug Application in 1950, intending to use cyclamate to mask the bitterness of certain drugs, such as antibiotics and pentobarbital. In 1958, cyclamate was designated as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) in the United States. It was marketed in tablet form as a tabletop sweetener for diabetics and in liquid form under brand names like Sucaryl, which remains available in non-U.S. markets. Cyclamate is 30–50 times sweeter than sugar, depending on its concentration, though its sweetness is not linearly proportional. It is the least potent of the commercially used artificial sweeteners. Some individuals report an unpleasant aftertaste, but it is generally less pronounced than that of saccharin or acesulfame potassium. Cyclamate is often used synergistically with other artificial sweeteners, particularly saccharin, in a common 10:1 cyclamate-to-saccharin ratio to mask the off-tastes of both. It is less expensive than most sweeteners, including sucralose, and is stable under heating. Chemically, cyclamate is the sodium or calcium salt of cyclamic acid (cyclohexanesulfamic acid). It is synthesized through the sulfonation of cyclohexylamine, which can be achieved by reacting cyclohexylamine with sulfamic acid or sulfur trioxide. In 1966, a study revealed that certain intestinal bacteria could desulfonate cyclamate, producing cyclohexylamine, a compound suspected of chronic toxicity in animals. Subsequent research in 1969 found that a common 10:1 cyclamate-to-saccharin mixture increased the incidence of bladder cancer in rats. Specifically, eight out of 240 rats fed this mixture at levels equivalent to humans consuming 350 cans of diet soda per day developed bladder tumors. Other studies implicated cyclohexylamine in testicular atrophy in mice. On October 18, 1969, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), citing the Delaney Amendment, banned the sale of cyclamate in the United States. The United Kingdom followed suit the next year. Abbott Laboratories contested the findings, claiming their own studies could not replicate the 1969 results. In 1973, Abbott petitioned the FDA to lift the ban, but this request was denied in 1980 by FDA Commissioner Jere Goyan. A second petition was filed in 1982 by Abbott Labs and the Calorie Control Council, a lobbying group for the diet foods industry. While the FDA has stated that a review of all available evidence does not implicate cyclamate as a carcinogen in mice or rats, it remains banned in U.S. food products. The petition is currently held in abeyance, though it is unclear whether this is at Abbott's request or due to insufficient evidence as determined by the FDA. Cyclamate is approved as a sweetener in over 55 countries. For example, the Canadian version of the brand-name sweetener Sweet'N Low contains cyclamate, whereas the U.S. version includes saccharin. Similarly, Sugar Twin, a cyclamate-based sweetener in Canada, contains saccharin in the United States. Animal studies, including those on mice and primates, have reported irreversible testicular atrophy and potential impacts on seminal vesicle function. However, the possible negative effects on male reproductive ability or function may fall outside the scope of committees tasked with evaluating product safety based solely on life expectancy and cancer rates. Since reduced testosterone levels are thought to correlate with a decreased incidence of certain cancers (e.g., testicular cancer) and increased life expectancy, substances that impair testosterone production may be more easily classified as safe under these criteria. Cyclamates appear to affect cells involved in sperm production, raising questions about their potential to damage male reproductive DNA. However, there is currently no direct evidence to confirm or refute this possibility.
